extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, screenwriting students, and general readers researching spec scripts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on writing and marketing a spec (unsolicited) screenplay intended to showcase a writer's storytelling talent and attract producers or buyers. Covers what to include/avoid in the script and common routes to get it read and sold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-commissioned / unsolicited status
rubrics_metrics.description: A spec script, also known as a speculative screenplay, is a non-commissioned and unsolicited screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spec scripts are written without prior request by a producer or studio; they are created in the hope the script will be optioned or purchased by a producer, production company, or studio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose — showcase storytelling ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The sole purpose of a spec script (selling script) is to showcase a screenwriter's talent of telling a story through action and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A spec is intended to demonstrate the writer's narrative skill and voice rather than serve as a production-ready document. The writing should highlight story, character, pacing, and dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize storytelling; avoid cinematography/directing details
rubrics_metrics.description: A spec script focuses more on the storytelling itself, while focus on cinematography and other directing aspects should rarely, if ever, be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including detailed camera directions, shot compositions, or directorial commands is an anti-pattern for specs; such videographic/technical directions are more appropriate in later drafts or shooting scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defer videographic and technical directions until later drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Videographic and technical directions are often added in the later drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep early/spec drafts lean on technical instructions so the script remains a demonstration of story and character; production-specific guidance can be layered in after the script attracts development interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format/readability difference from shooting/production scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: A spec script reads differently from a shooting script or production script in that it focuses more on storytelling and less on production detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should format and write a spec to be readable for readers interested in story (producers, development executives), not as a set of production instructions for directors/crew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an agent and building 'heat' to attract buyers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the writer has an agent, the agent will identify a number of prospective buyers and attempt to build up 'heat' under the script.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents may send the script simultaneously to multiple prospective buyers (from independents to studio execs) to spark interest or a bidding war; having representation can change marketing strategy and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of studio database rejection / potential for later discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: If the script is not picked up, it may be in studio databases and development executives may have marked it as 'passed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being passed in studio systems can limit immediate chances, but a well-regarded unproduced spec can still surface on lists of notable unproduced scripts (e.g., The Black List) and eventually attract interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality can lead to writing assignments or development deals
rubrics_metrics.description: If a spec script is not picked up but the writing is good, the screenwriter may be offered a writing assignment or a 'development deal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studios or producers may hire the writer to write another original script or adapt a book/idea, turning a strong spec into paid work even if that specific script is not produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative marketing avenues — competitions and online posting
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside the traditional route of finding an agent, writers can enter competitions (e.g., Nicholl Fellowship, Final Draft's Big Break) or post their screenplay on online posting services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contests can increase visibility and legitimacy; online posting services allow writers to receive feedback and, if endorsed by the service, be posted publicly to attract producers. These are alternative strategies to reach buyers when not represented.
